stimulusBlocks.attribution: John Locke, English philosopher, Second Treatise of Government, 1690
stimulusBlocks.citation: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, sections 95 and 222. Project Gutenberg eBook #7370.
stimulusBlocks.note: Locke uses “property” to mean people's lives, liberties, and estates. The legislative is the lawmaking power.
stimulusBlocks.text:
MEN being, as has been said, by nature, all free, equal, and independent, no one can be put out of this estate, and subjected to the political power of another, without his own consent. . . .

. . . whenever the legislators endeavour to take away, and destroy the property of the people, or to reduce them to slavery under arbitrary power, they put themselves into a state of war with the people, who are thereupon absolved from any farther obedience . . . . Whensoever therefore the legislative shall transgress this fundamental rule of society; and either by ambition, fear, folly or corruption, endeavour to grasp themselves, or put into the hands of any other, an absolute power over the lives, liberties, and estates of the people; by this breach of trust they forfeit the power the people had put into their hands for quite contrary ends, and it devolves to the people, who have a right to resume their original liberty . . . .

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Mary Wollstonecraft, English writer, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792
stimulusBlocks.citation: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, chs. 3–4. Project Gutenberg eBook #3420.
stimulusBlocks.note: Wollstonecraft is responding to the French Enlightenment writer Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who argued that women should be educated to please men. Bracketed words replace “they.”
stimulusBlocks.text:
It is time to effect a revolution in female manners, time to restore to them their lost dignity, and make them, as a part of the human species, labour by reforming themselves to reform the world. . . .

[Women] would be more respectable members of society, and discharge the important duties of life by the light of their own reason. "Educate women like men," says Rousseau, "and the more they resemble our sex the less power will they have over us." This is the very point I aim at. I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.1 key concept: Enlightenment ideas and religious ideals influenced reform movements, including the abolition of slavery, the end of serfdom, and the expansion of political rights
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing reform movements influenced by Enlightenment ideas, 1780–1900
stimulusBlocks.text:
Enlightenment arguments about natural rights gave reformers a powerful language. Abolitionists, many of them also motivated by religious belief, pressed Britain to end its slave trade in 1807 and to abolish slavery in most of its empire in 1833. Russia emancipated its serfs in 1861. In 1848, activists meeting at Seneca Falls, New York, demanded rights for women, including the vote.

Change came slowly and unevenly. The United States ended slavery only in 1865 after a civil war, Brazil in 1888. New Zealand became the first country to allow women to vote in national elections in 1893.

questions.prompt: The second paragraph best supports which claim?
choices: Reforms happened everywhere at once

Reforms spread slowly and unevenly
questions.explanation: Dates from 1833 to 1893 show uneven change.
choiceExplanations: The dates differ widely.
Many reforms succeeded.
Brazil abolished slavery late, in 1888.
Dates from 1833 to 1893 show uneven change.
questions.distinguisher: The dates range from 1807 to 1893, so change was not simultaneous.

questions.prompt: Locke's argument differs most sharply from which earlier justification for royal authority?

questions.explanation: Divine right made a king accountable to God alone, while Locke made rulers accountable to the people who consented to be governed.

I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.
